title: Verbal Reasoning: Words, Statements, and Inference

questions.question: What exactly does a Statement and Assumption question ask you to judge?
options: The claim that definitely follows after the statement
The unstated premise the author must believe for the statement to make sense
Which of two events caused the other
Whether the statement is factually true in the real world
questions.rationale: An assumption is the hidden premise the author must already believe before writing the statement. Conclusions and causes are different judgement families, and the real-world truth of the statement is never in question.

questions.question: In exam logic, the statement "some students are athletes" guarantees which of the following?
options: At least one student is an athlete — and it is still possible that all students are athletes
questions.rationale: "Some" means only "at least one"; it never denies the possibility that "all" holds. Reading "some" as "some but not all" is the classic verbal reasoning error.

questions.question: An option that introduces a new fact the statement never mentioned receives which verdict in the elimination method?
questions.rationale: Options are tested as Supported, Contradicted, or Out of scope. An option that invents facts the statement is silent about is out of scope and must be eliminated.

questions.question: Statement: "Only members may enter the reading room." Which option definitely follows?
options: Non-members may not enter the reading room
Members may not use the other rooms
All visitors to the building are members
The reading room is always full of members
questions.rationale: "Only members" makes membership a necessary condition, so anyone who is not a member is excluded — option A is the exact meaning. The other options add facts about other rooms, visitors, or crowds that the statement never gives.

questions.question: Statement: "Regular exercise may reduce the risk of heart disease." Why is the option "Regular exercise will reduce the risk of heart disease" wrong?
options: It reverses the direction of the claim
It is true in the real world, so it cannot be tested
questions.rationale: A supported option must match the statement's strength or be weaker. Converting a possibility (may) into a certainty (will) strengthens the claim, so the option fails.

questions.question: Which term describes a belief that is hidden but required before the statement makes sense?
questions.rationale: An assumption lives before the statement — the author must believe it for the text to work. Conclusions and inferences come after the statement, and an implication is only a suggestion inside the wording.

questions.question: Based on the typical exam distribution, which verbal topic usually carries the most questions in the reasoning section?
questions.rationale: The lesson's bar chart shows Statement and Conclusion with the largest typical share (about 5 questions). It is also the topic where elimination removes wrong options fastest.

questions.question: In the statement "Only graduates are eligible for this post", the word "only" establishes graduation as:
options: A sufficient condition — every graduate is eligible
A necessary condition — a non-graduate is not eligible
An irrelevant detail about the post
questions.rationale: "Only X" makes X necessary: no one outside X qualifies. But necessary is not sufficient — graduates may still fail other requirements, so option A overstates what "only" gives.

questions.question: Which single verdict must an option receive in order to be accepted as correct?
questions.rationale: Only options fully supported by the statement's exact wording survive. Contradicted and out-of-scope options are eliminated, and real-world plausibility is never a test.

questions.question: For the statement "You should carry an umbrella — the forecast says rain", the belief "the forecast is generally reliable" is:
questions.rationale: The advice only makes sense if the speaker trusts the forecast — an unstated premise needed before the statement works, which is exactly an assumption. The conclusion is the advice itself, stated after the text.
